title: Advertising jobs, plentiful work then, and demanding his price
summary: He describes playing in store advertising and athletic club jobs, how musicians used to be only musicians, and insisting on pay instead of food and drink.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Getting paid: wages, scale and the pay envelope

blocks.x: Yes sir. And then I had a Petone's, uh, fighting arena, the fifth water athletic club. Every Friday. Where was that? That street? That athletic club on the domain between Decatur and Charlotte. And then I had a, uh, on the downtown side of the bank. Cause it was called the Fifth Water Athletic Club. That was every Friday. I had, uh, Fry's Grocery on Canal and Villeary, Food Store. It was advertised for them. I think it was every Tuesday or Wednesday. And... You got on a truck there? Yeah, on a truck. And, uh, it was filled up pretty good. It was filled up pretty good all the way. Yeah. Different places we'd go play a dance. You see, plenty of bands at that time. You see when the holidays would come along? Mm-hm. And, uh, people would be like crazy around and looking for a band. Yes, please. Now they've got too many bands. Yeah. All of the youngsons. No jobs. All of the youngsons go to school now. They go with their school band and play for these dances for nothing. Mm-hm. And, uh, let's shed a side planet place. I guess so. The music box, they shed a side planet place. Yeah. So that's what a musician can't make a head with. You see when I first started playing, every man is on trade. Musicians played music. Carpenter, he was a carpenter, he stayed in his place, he ain't coming my way. Slater and different other people, they stood on their side. Well that gave me a chance to play music. Musicians played nightclubs and all like that. Well he's filling his arm play. They had work for them. But now the carpenter's is playing music, Slater's, and the, what you call it, people, people working in the market, they're musicians too. Oh you find musicians all over. Now you ain't got no trouble looking for a band. You come at this corner, you don't find a band, go at this corner and get it. But when I was coming, it wasn't like that. You take and have work and have plenty of it. And you could demand your price. You know what people used to tell me? I want you to come over, you don't have to play nothing, just make a game of plenty noise, that's all. Oh I said, no indeed. I said, we don't do that kind of business. And if they wouldn't tell you that, they'd tell you, they wouldn't want to give you a big price. They said, we'll give you plenty of eating drinks. I worked for Sergeant Morrison, Captain Anderson, all them fellas, American Legion, you know. Yeah. Go out on the lake on a picnic. We're going to give you plenty of eating drinks. I said, well Cap, I'll tell you. I said, I eat and drink plenty at my house. Well sometime I might go to jail, we'll get you out. I said, I don't go to no jail. I said, because I'm a man, I stay to myself, I don't go look for no trouble. And if I see trouble and I try to get out the way from you, of course anybody can get in trouble. Yeah, that's right, sometime. But I said, I don't believe you, I'll be able to cash back on you. I said, the offers you give me, I said, I got to have my money, so I paid a mendo. So, let's forget about the eating and drinking. Well I'll play that job. You remember when Captain Anderson fell off that camp at the lake? I don't remember about that, no.
